garyk.core: old core of granite and gneiss under the interior (part of the First Land)

caren.summary: Caren is a fragment of the First Land: an old continental core (a craton) with the worn roots of an ancient mountain belt along it, split off when the First Land rifted and carried since by the Caren Plate at about a centimetre a year. It lies far inside its plate: no plate edge, no volcano and no active rift, only the small, scattered earthquakes of an old continent.

timeline.text: Caren's core forms: old continental crust with a thick, cold, buoyant root (a craton).

The core is caught in the First Land's assembly and an ancient mountain belt rises along it. Deep in the thickened crust rock melts into great bodies of granite that cool underground and never erupt; their fluids leave veins of tin, tungsten, silver, lead, zinc and copper around them. Coal swamps fill the basins at the belt's foot (320 to 300).
The belt wears down to its roots. Limestone and sandstone gather in the basins (marble where they were baked and squeezed), with beds of copper, lead and zinc from basin brines, ironstone and salt.
The First Land rifts apart and Caren is split off as a fragment.
Caren rides the Caren Plate to where it lies today; the plate has slowed to about a centimetre a year.
A great body from the sky strikes the old core and leaves a ringed structure 150 to 200 km across, long before any people: the Arluna Lakes lie in its trough.
A broad swell of the mantle lifts northern Caren into a plateau, without a volcano; the hard massifs of the old belt stand above it.

nudges.what: The gods steered the rift, so that the fragment split off took Caren's shape and came to rest where Caren lies.
nudges.evidence: an ordinary rifted margin: smooth coasts and wide shelves all round, and rocks that match the First Land's across the sea

nudges.what: The gods placed a small plume beneath northern Caren; under the thick old crust it lifts the land and never breaks through.
nudges.evidence: a broad dome of raised land, rivers cut down into it, warm springs, and no young volcanic rock

rocks.rock: white quartzite and massive white leucogranite (the Godstone, as Caren's people call it)
rocks.note: the hardest rocks of the ancient belt: they weather very slowly, into smooth domes and bare white walls
tin and tungsten nearest the granite; silver, lead, zinc and copper in veins farther out
banded white and grey marble, the classic building stone; coal in the old foothill basins

rocks.rock: limestone and sandstone over the old core
rocks.note: fertile; caves, sinkholes and springs in the limestone; copper beds, lead and zinc, ironstone and salt in the old basins

ores.source: the granites' own fluids, close to the granite

ores.ore: silver, lead, zinc and copper in veins

caren.earthquakes: small and scattered, as on any old continent far from a plate edge: the young uplift is taken up on many small faults (old faults of the ancient belt, and the swell's margins), mostly under magnitude 4, now and then 4 to 5, rarely 5 to 6, never more

history.text: Beneath the plates the mantle turns over in two broad upwellings on opposite sides of the world, with cold sinking sheets between them; plumes rise from the upwellings' margins and stay fixed while the plates pass over them.

Old cores, swept together over the sinking mantle between the upwellings, collide and weld into the First Land; their seams become the inland belts of Gaffa, Khohalis and Demani and the old core under Garyk.

Lying long over the mantle like a lid, the First Land comes to sit above one of the upwellings, which domes it up and rifts it apart around Garyk; the rifts become passive, smooth coasts with wide shelves.
Gaffa, Khohalis and Demani break away from Garyk's side and drift together to the far side of the world, some twelve thousand kilometres, each turning about its own pole; Garyk stays behind.

Leading edges override sinking sea floor: coastal ranges, volcanoes and island arcs grow along them. The sea floor that still trails a sinking slab is pulled fast; Gaffa, Khohalis and Demani, whose slabs are gone and whose edges now ride over the sea floor ahead, have slowed to a few centimetres a year.

Plumes rising from the upwellings' margins build the open-sea archipelagos; each plate carries the older volcanoes away along its motion, where they sink into lines of seamounts, oldest farthest from the plume.
The Northern Garyk Sea Plate closes on Garyk; its northern ranges rise along the seam.
Wear and the slow rebound of the crust soften the old belts to rounded hills and lower the young ranges.

Caren, an old core with an ancient mountain belt from the assembly along it, is split off from the First Land's rim as a fragment and rides the Caren Plate some 9000 km to where it lies today. Its plate has no sinking slab left to pull it and has slowed to about a centimetre a year.
